subject: bio
title: Enzymes
subtitle: Enzyme action, factors affecting rate, inhibition and immobilised enzymes.
concept: Enzymes are globular proteins that act as biological catalysts — they lower activation energy by forming an enzyme-substrate complex at the active site.
The lock-and-key and induced fit models describe substrate binding; only substrates with a complementary shape bind.
Inhibitors reduce enzyme activity; competitive inhibitors compete for the active site, non-competitive inhibitors alter the active site shape.

notes.heading: Mechanism of Enzyme Action
items: Enzymes are globular proteins that act as biological catalysts — they lower the activation energy of a reaction without being consumed. Each enzyme has an active site with a specific 3D shape complementary to one substrate (or a small group of structurally similar substrates).

Lock-and-key model: the substrate fits the active site precisely, like a key in a lock. Induced fit model: the active site changes shape slightly on substrate binding to achieve a better fit — this is now the preferred model. The enzyme–substrate complex forms, products are released, and the enzyme is regenerated unchanged.

notes.heading: Factors Affecting Rate
items: Temperature: rate increases up to the optimum (≈37 °C in humans) because more molecules exceed the activation energy. Above the optimum, excessive vibration breaks the hydrogen bonds and other non-covalent bonds maintaining tertiary structure — the active site changes shape (denaturation) and the enzyme cannot bind substrate.

pH: each enzyme has an optimum pH. Changes in pH alter the ionisation of amino acid R-groups in the active site, disrupting the bonds that maintain its shape. Extremes cause irreversible denaturation.

Substrate concentration [S]: rate increases as [S] rises — more enzyme–substrate complexes form per second. At Vmax (maximum velocity), all active sites are permanently occupied (saturated); adding more substrate has no effect.
Enzyme concentration: increasing [E] increases rate proportionally (more active sites available), provided substrate is not limiting.

notes.heading: Inhibitors
items: Competitive inhibitors have a shape similar to the substrate and compete for the active site. The effect is reversible and can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration — at high [S], substrate out-competes the inhibitor.

Non-competitive (allosteric) inhibitors bind to a separate allosteric site, causing a conformational change in the active site so the substrate can no longer fit. Increasing [S] does not restore activity — Vmax is reduced.
Irreversible inhibitors form permanent covalent bonds with the enzyme (e.g. nerve agents that block acetylcholinesterase). The enzyme is permanently inactivated.

notes.heading: Immobilised Enzymes
items: Immobilised enzymes are attached to an inert support (e.g. alginate beads, cellulose fibres) so they can be easily separated from the product.
Advantages: (1) enzyme is reusable — reduces cost; (2) product is uncontaminated by enzyme; (3) allows continuous processing in a column reactor.
Industrial examples: lactase on beads to produce lactose-free milk; glucose isomerase to convert glucose to fructose (used in food industry).

definitions.body: The region of an enzyme molecule with a specific 3D shape that binds the substrate to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
Model of enzyme action where the active site changes shape slightly to fit the substrate more precisely upon binding.
A molecule with a similar shape to the substrate that occupies the active site, preventing substrate binding. Effect can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration.
A molecule that binds to an allosteric site on the enzyme, changing the shape of the active site so the substrate can no longer bind.
Permanent change in 3D shape of an enzyme due to disruption of bonds maintaining tertiary structure; the enzyme loses its activity.

workedExamples.q: Explain the effect of increasing temperature beyond the optimum on enzyme activity.

steps.text: Above the optimum temperature, the increased kinetic energy causes the R-groups of amino acids to vibrate excessively.
The hydrogen bonds (and other non-covalent bonds) maintaining the tertiary structure are disrupted/broken.
The active site changes shape — it is no longer complementary to the substrate. The enzyme is denatured and substrate cannot bind, so the reaction rate falls to zero.

mistakes: Saying temperature 'destroys the enzyme' — say it 'denatures' the enzyme and explain bond disruption.
Confusing competitive (active site, overcome by [S]) with non-competitive (allosteric site, not overcome by [S]).
Stating that above Vmax, adding more enzyme has no effect — it does if substrate is limiting.
tips: For inhibitor questions: if increasing [S] restores activity → competitive; if not → non-competitive.
Denaturation: always state which bonds are disrupted (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds), not 'all bonds broken'.
Immobilised enzymes: always give TWO advantages for full marks.

flashcards.q: What is the induced fit model?
flashcards.a: The active site changes shape slightly on binding the substrate to achieve a better fit, forming the enzyme-substrate complex.

flashcards.q: How does a competitive inhibitor work?
flashcards.a: It has a similar shape to the substrate and binds to the active site, blocking substrate entry. Effect is reduced by increasing [S].

flashcards.q: What happens to enzyme activity above the optimum temperature?
flashcards.a: Denaturation — H-bonds and other bonds in the tertiary structure break, the active site changes shape, and the substrate no longer fits.
The maximum rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction, achieved when all active sites are saturated with substrate.

flashcards.q: Name two advantages of immobilised enzymes.
flashcards.a: (1) Enzyme can be reused (cost-effective). (2) Product is not contaminated by enzyme.

flashcards.q: How does pH affect enzyme activity?
flashcards.a: Changes in pH alter ionisation of amino acid R-groups, disrupting bonds in the active site; each enzyme has an optimum pH.

questions.q: Which correctly describes a non-competitive inhibitor?
opts: Binds active site; effect overcome by high [S]
Binds allosteric site; cannot be overcome by high [S]
questions.exp: Non-competitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site and change the active site shape; increasing [S] does not restore activity.

questions.q: At Vmax, what is limiting enzyme activity?
questions.exp: At Vmax all active sites are occupied — increasing substrate concentration further has no effect.

questions.q: Which bonds are primarily disrupted when an enzyme is denatured by high temperature?
opts: Hydrogen bonds and other non-covalent bonds
questions.exp: Denaturation disrupts hydrogen bonds and other non-covalent bonds maintaining tertiary structure — peptide bonds (primary structure) are not broken.

questions.q: Lactase is immobilised in alginate beads. What is one advantage?
opts: Eliminates the need for optimum pH
questions.exp: Immobilised enzymes can be recovered and reused, making the process more cost-effective.

questions.q: An inhibitor reduces enzyme activity. Adding more substrate fully restores the rate. What type of inhibitor is it?
questions.exp: Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site; adding more substrate outcompetes the inhibitor and restores Vmax.

recall: Explain how temperature affects enzyme activity, referring to bonds.
Explain why enzyme activity reaches a maximum (Vmax) as [S] increases.
State two uses of immobilised enzymes.

summary.label: High temp
